summary.text: Twice-born from the lightning that slew Semele at Thebes, Dionysus wandered the world with his nurses and maenads — driving Lycurgus mad in Thrace, turning Tyrrhenian pirates into dolphins, shattering Pentheus who denied him, granting and revoking Midas' golden touch, and taking Ariadne from Naxos to be his bride among the stars.

chapters.title: Twice-born at Thebes
chapters.text: Semele daughter of Cadmus lay with Zeus until Hera's trick brought the lightning; the god sewed the unborn child in his thigh, and Dionysus entered the world — though poets dispute whether Persephone or Semele was his first mother.
chapters.citation: Hes. Th. 940–942; Apollod. 3.4.3; Ov. Met. 3.253–315; Hyg. Fab. 167

chapters.title: Wanderings and resistance
chapters.text: Lycurgus of Thrace was the first to drive the god's nurses from Nysa with an ox-goad, until Dionysus fled to Thetis and the gods blinded the king. Tyrrhenian sailors who tried to sell the beautiful stranger found mast and sail become vine and ivy, and themselves dolphins in the sea.

chapters.title: Pentheus and the maenads
chapters.text: Returning to his mother's city, Dionysus found Pentheus denying the new god; he drove the Theban women to frenzy on Cithaeron, and Agave the king's mother tore her son apart with her bare hands, thinking him a lion.

chapters.title: Bridegroom and judge
chapters.text: On Naxos he received Ariadne abandoned by Theseus — Homer makes Artemis slay her on his word, while other poets crown her among the stars as his wife. In Phrygia King Midas won the golden touch from Bacchus and washed the curse away in the river; on Tmolus he preferred Pan's pipes to Apollo's lyre and wore ass's ears for his judgment.
